From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. After the service, Legion members, RCMP, Sea Cadets, Air Cadets and youth organizations included Cubs, Scouts, Voyageurs, Guides and Brownies paraded to the cenotaph for wreath-laying, before returning to the Legion hall to lay wreaths at its cairn. items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. tribunal overturns $100,000 fine against X over intimate image
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal has overturned a $100,000 penalty against social media platform X for failing to delete an intimate image posted without a woman’s consent, ruling that blocking access to it in Canada was a reasonable step under provincial law. The tribunal said the law did not make X liable after it blocked Canadian access to the image, which remained available outside Canada. The decision reversed a September 2025 penalty for failing to comply with an order to delete it. The tribunal accepted X’s argument that requiring worldwide removal could interfere with other countries’ legal systems and cited a 2024 Australian case as persuasive but not binding. Outgoing B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma criticized X’s refusal to remove the image and said governments may need to strengthen laws or pursue legal action. The tribunal also rejected X’s request to require the complainant to pay more than US$100,000 in legal fees.

items.title: [thestar.com] McGill report finds deepfake network spreading false Canada-U.S. trade claims
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. Many focused on Canada’s trade dispute with the United States. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. items.title: [bbc.co.uk] UK court convicts two Iranians in plot targeting dissident journalists
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A jury at Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, on Nov. 12 of assisting an Iranian intelligence service by conducting surveillance on critics of Tehran in Britain. Sepahvand was also convicted of conduct linked to preparing a violent attack; Manesh was acquitted of that separate charge. A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, was acquitted of all charges. The targets included Iran International journalists Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, a founder of UK Lawyers for Israel, and a media production professional. British prosecutors and counterterrorism police said Sepahvand acted under the direction of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) or intermediaries, and that the men were offered rewards for sending information to contacts in Iran. Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in espionage in Britain. Police described the verdicts as the first convictions of Iranian nationals under Britain’s 2023 National Security Act. The court is due to sentence Sepahvand and Manesh at the Old Bailey on Dec. 17.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Prince Harry and five others seek permission to appeal in Daily Mail privacy case
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, and five other public figures have applied for permission to appeal the dismissal of their privacy claims against Associated Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday. Their application, filed on Friday, Nov. 6, challenges both the High Court’s rejection of the claims and a later order on the publisher’s legal costs. The claimants alleged that journalists or people working for the publisher used unlawful information-gathering methods, including voicemail interception and deception; Associated Newspapers denied the allegations. After an 11-week trial, High Court judge Matthew Nicklin ruled on July 7 that none of the seven claimants had proved unlawful information gathering. He accepted journalists’ explanations that the articles came from lawful sources and said suspicion alone could not establish the claims. The claimants say the rulings are “legally and factually flawed”. In August, Nicklin ordered an initial payment of £9,544,355 toward the publisher’s costs, with the final amount to be determined at a separate hearing. He ordered costs to be assessed on an indemnity basis, which can allow greater recovery. Associated Newspapers estimated its defence costs at about £34.5 million by July 9. The Court of Appeal must first decide whether to grant permission to appeal.

items.title: [sci.news] Cambridge study finds comets rarely delivered life’s ingredients to Earth
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A University of Cambridge-led study finds it was extremely unlikely that comets delivered enough hydrogen cyanide, a chemical used in proposed pathways to life, to early Earth. The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric entry and impacts. The team says most impacts would destroy the molecule or fail to leave it at a useful concentration. Of the researchers’ 100,000 simulated histories, 54% included no comet impact that delivered hydrogen cyanide at concentrations considered sufficient for prebiotic chemistry. Comet delivery was more likely on Mars, where lower gravity and a thinner atmosphere make successful impacts more feasible, but the study does not establish that it happened there. The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. items._excerpt: A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology (sciencefeatured.com). The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began (sciencefeatured.com). The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity (sciencefeatured.com). The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions (sciencefeatured.com). Study sample: The analysis included several thousand participants with healthy memory and thinking abilities at the outset; models accounted for factors including education, smoking, depression and chronic illness (sciencefeatured.com). Cognitive tests: Participants completed word-list recall tests to assess memory and counting and subtraction tasks to assess executive function (sciencefeatured.com). Exercise research: Montreal neuropsychologist Louis Bherer said participants in his lab’s physical and cognitive exercise programs showed improvements in attention and response speed after training, while memory changes took longer (nautil.us).

items.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.

items.title: [e.vnexpress.net] Travel technology provider Amadeus breach exposes 46,000 Singapore Airlines records
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Singapore Airlines said about 46,000 booking records may have been accessed in a breach at travel technology provider Amadeus, potentially exposing passenger names, booking references, itineraries and booking classes. About 620 records may also have included email addresses, phone numbers, travel-document details and KrisFlyer membership numbers. The airline said payment information was not exposed, bookings were not changed and its own systems were not breached. The unauthorized access involved booking data from August 2023 to September 2026. Cathay Pacific reported about 53,000 affected bookings, Japan Airlines about 92,000 affected customers and All Nippon Airways 37,800 affected records; Qantas is still checking whether its bookings were affected. Amadeus said it fixed the vulnerability and strengthened monitoring. Singapore Airlines is contacting customers with upcoming travel to change their booking references, while Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Commission said it is investigating.

items.content_html:

Perry Johnson Companies, a Nevada-based medical services firm, agreed to pay $300,000 and overhaul its cybersecurity practices to settle claims by attorneys general in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York and Michigan over a 2023 breach that exposed data on more than 13 million people. If Perry Johnson does not complete the required reforms, it could owe the states another $9.7 million.

items.title: [brecorder.com] Suspected Gulf tanker strike kills seafarer as Iran reports fires
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A seafarer was killed when an unidentified projectile struck the Greek-managed, Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Velos Sapphire in the Gulf on Thursday, November 5, its operator, Velos Tankers, said. The vessel was sailing empty toward Bahrain. The explosion started a fire that the crew extinguished, and the ship later reached Bahrain’s Khalifa Bin Salman Port. The attacker has not been identified. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz by an unauthorized route. Iranian media had reported the previous day that five tankers and a tugboat were on fire. Maritime security agencies had not confirmed Iran’s mine-strike claims; the United States has said it cleared mines from the strait. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported an explosion aboard another tanker off Oman. Its crew were safe, and the vessel continued under its own power. The waterway normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption. Iran is seeking to restrict traffic, while the United States blockades Iranian ports and escorts tankers. Velos Tankers said it would launch an investigation and was still assessing damage to the vessel’s hull.
